item.title: inDepth I Welfare cover axed
item.description: THE Government has ended a controversial social welfare insurance scheme after paying about $60 million in taxpayers’ money over eight years, with only $33.8 million reaching beneficiaries through direct claims. item.content:encoded:
THE Government has ended a controversial social welfare insurance scheme after paying about $60 million in taxpayers’ money over eight years, with only $33.8 million reaching beneficiaries through direct claims.

Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week that the decision to discontinue the scheme was fiscally responsible and necessary, arguing that too much public money was being absorbed by insurance costs rather than reaching vulnerable Fijians.

The scheme, introduced in 2018, was initially designed to increase insurance penetration among civil servants and social welfare recipients. Civil servants were later removed because of the high cost of maintaining their coverage.

Under the scheme, Government paid quarterly premiums for eligible welfare recipients, covering areas including term life, funeral expenses, personal accidents and fire.

But Ms Kiran said the numbers showed a significant mismatch between what Government paid and what beneficiaries received.

“Over the past eight years, the Government has diligently paid approximately $60 million in hard-earned taxpayers’ funds to FijiCare Insurance as premiums,” she said.

“However, a deeper dive into the metrics reveals a stark and troubling imbalance.”

Of the $60 million paid in premiums, only $33.8 million was paid out to citizens as direct claims.

In 2023-2024, Government paid $7.1 million in premiums but received claims payouts totalling only $3.8 million.

The following year, premiums increased to $7.2 million while payouts remained at $3.8 million.

In 2025-2026, premiums rose again to $7.7 million, but claims fell to $3 million.

Ms Kiran said the figures demonstrated that the insurance model was failing to deliver value for public money.

“On average, a mere 56 per cent of the total funds paid out by the Government ended up in the hands of the beneficiaries.

“The remaining 44 per cent did not serve our poor. Instead, it was absorbed by administrative friction, overheads and private corporate margins.”

Ms Kiran said Government had been spending roughly $7 million annually to cover about 100,000 welfare recipients, yet only about 5000 claims were processed each year.

“We are paying massive premium blocks for a system where 95 per cent of the covered population see no tangible touchpoint or benefit in any given year.”

She argued that the scheme was particularly inefficient because most recipients did not directly benefit from the insurance during any given year.

Ms Kiran said the data also showed that the primary beneficiaries were often family members rather than elderly welfare recipients themselves.

The scheme provided one-off assistance for life and funeral costs, with payments ranging from $1500 for those under 60 to $500 for seniors aged between 60 and 69.

Fire and personal accident cover provided up to $3000.

However, Ms Kiran pointed to the extremely low number of personal accident claims as evidence of underutilisation.

“Personal accidents under this scheme are extremely rare.

“To highlight this, the entire 2022-2023 financial year, there were only four paid-out accident claims across the nation, costing a total of $10,500.”

Government promises safety-net alternatives

Ms Kiran rejected concerns that ending the insurance scheme would leave welfare recipients without protection.

“I want to assure this House that removing this insurance scheme will have minimal to no impact on the existing social welfare recipients.”

She said Government would continue providing direct assistance through six major social welfare programs.

For the 2026-2027 financial year, the Government has allocated $184 million across the programs.

This includes $46.46 million for the Family Assistance Scheme, more than $18 million for the Child Protection Allowance, more than $82 million for the Social Pension Scheme, over $420,000 for food allowance for rural pregnant mothers, more than $18 million for allowances for persons with disabilities and over $14 million for the Transport Assistance Scheme.

Ms Kiran said the Government believed direct assistance provided a more effective way of supporting vulnerable people than paying large insurance premiums.

item.title: Khan moves to halt asset forfeiture proceedings
item.description: INMATE Imran Khan has filed an urgent High Court application seeking to stay State forfeiture proceedings and preserve assets subject to an active appeal. Khan, currently serving a prison sentence, alongside second appellant Deborah Kim, filed an affidavit on August 21 requesting an order to halt further forfeiture actions by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) pending their Court of Appeal
item.content:encoded:
INMATE Imran Khan has filed an urgent High Court application seeking to stay State forfeiture proceedings and preserve assets subject to an active appeal.

Khan, currently serving a prison sentence, alongside second appellant Deborah Kim, filed an affidavit on August 21 requesting an order to halt further forfeiture actions by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) pending their Court of Appeal case.

The application stems from a February 20, 2026, judgment by Justice Senileba Waqainabete-Levaci. The court issued an unexplained wealth declaration and permanent restraint orders over $404,840.34 in a Bred Bank account under Reliable Computers, a Valelevu residential property, and four vehicles.

According to the application, Khan states that while his lawyer only learned of the DPP’s new forfeiture application through media reports, finalising forfeiture before their appeal is heard would render their legal challenge meaningless.

The appellants argue the original ruling erred by relying on speculative opinion evidence without cross-examination and failing to conduct adequate financial analysis.

Khan assured the court they are not seeking the release of the assets, offering to maintain current restraint orders to preserve status quo until the appeal concludes.

item.title: Avoidable backlash
item.description: THE confusion and backlash now erupting across Fiji’s key tourist source markets as a result of the 5 per cent Tourism Services Tax (TST) was avoidable and was flagged to the Government in detail months before the controversial tax was gazetted. The FHTA had continuously raised concerns since the announcement of the levy, and had also proposed simpler and less disruptive ways to support Fiji Airwa
item.content:encoded:
THE confusion and backlash now erupting across Fiji’s key tourist source markets as a result of the 5 per cent Tourism Services Tax (TST) was avoidable and was flagged to the Government in detail months before the controversial tax was gazetted.

The FHTA had continuously raised concerns since the announcement of the levy, and had also proposed simpler and less disruptive ways to support Fiji Airways directly rather than a blunt tax bolted onto the wider tourism supply chain.

According to the FHTA, the Australian Travel Industry Association had called the tax’s retrospective application to existing bookings “an absolute no-go”, and accused Fiji of a fundamental misunderstanding of how the travel booking ecosystem, worked.

“We tried to make this work from day one and we were ignored at every turn,” FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said in a statement.

“We asked that pre-booked and paid holidays be exempted, the same treatment given under the old Service Turnover Tax. We asked for clarity on the sunset clause. Both requests were left out of the final Gazette, without explanation.”

She said they had also asked for a minimum of four weeks between the release of the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service’s Standard Interpretation Guidelines and the tax’s implementation date, given how much narrower the TST’s scope was compared with the STT it replaced.

“The guidelines were not finalised until yesterday, 10 days before the tax takes effect on September 1.

“We handed government a clear, specific warning of exactly how complicated this was going to be to administer.

“That warning was not heard, or it was heard and dismissed.

“Either way, the result is the mess our travel partners are now scrambling to clean up, with days rather than weeks to do it.”

Ms Lockington said agents managing multi-resort itineraries had described a process with no consistent collection method, forcing them to re-invoice wholesalers, re-invoice clients, and reconcile bookings that were settled months ago.

She said New Zealand agents had raised the same alarm at the Fiji roadshow events in Christchurch last week.

“Tourism Fiji and this industry have spent years and a great deal of money building Fiji’s name as a credible, well-run destination in markets with no shortage of alternatives.

“That reputation is being damaged this week, not because of the tax itself, but because Government would not listen when we told them exactly how to avoid this outcome.”

She said with the guidelines only finalised last week, travel agents, wholesalers and tour operators now had a little over a week to overhaul booking systems, invoicing processes and client communications before the tax takes effect.

“Our industry is not against Fiji investing in its own aviation sector.

“What we needed was consultation, time and clarity, and we asked for all three, repeatedly, well before this became a crisis.”

item.title: Fiji eyes green aviation
item.description: FIJI’s aviation sector serves as a primary backbone to the national economy, providing a vital bridge for international tourism, regional trade and island to island connectivity. However, with growth comes a responsibility to ensure that with each transition, counter measures are in place to address high cost of aviation fuel, carbon dioxide emissions and an overall environmentally conscious strat
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’s aviation sector serves as a primary backbone to the national economy, providing a vital bridge for international tourism, regional trade and island to island connectivity.

However, with growth comes a responsibility to ensure that with each transition, counter measures are in place to address high cost of aviation fuel, carbon dioxide emissions and an overall environmentally conscious strategy towards sustainability.

This is one of the many reasons investments in the sector’s sustainability is a focus that government past, present and future continue to prioritise.

This year, however, the need for sustainable fuel efficient and low-cost measures were ramped up especially with the war in the Middle East, which placed immense pressure on every industry to find better and less costly solutions.

In Parliament last week, Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation Viliame Gavoka introduced the Civil Aviation Master Plan 2026 to 2031 – a strategic framework designed to set the pace for industry stakeholders committed to a more sustainable future.

Essentially, the Civil Aviation Master Plan 2026 to 2031, Mr Gavoka explained, outlined Fiji’s commitment to reducing carbon dioxide emissions through sustainable practices by each stakeholder. He said this was further provided in the Fiji State Action Plan developed in accordance with the International Civil Aviation Organisation Resolution A41-22.

“It outlines the protocol measures that Fiji is implementing to reduce carbon emissions from international aviation and contribute towards ICAO’s long-term aspirational goal of net-zero aviation emissions by 2050,” he said.

“The Action Plan identifies a range of measures, including fleet modernisation, improved air traffic management, airport energy efficiency, sustainable aviation fuels, and renewable energy infrastructure.”

Mr Gavoka explained one of the state entities paving the way was Fiji Airports through its new solar farm featuring a 3.25 megawatt solar power system at the Nadi International Airport where an estimated 2.5MW of electricity is consumed.

“When completed, the solar farm will generate sufficient renewable energy to meet current airport demand, thereby sustainably reducing reliance on conventional electricity sources while strengthening operational resilience and long-term energy security.

“Fiji Airports has advised that approximately 25 per cent surplus generated capacity will be available during peak periods, creating opportunities to support future airport development and contribute excess electricity back to the national grid.”

He said the Master Plan also recognised that future airports must be safe, resilient, technologically advanced and environmentally sustainable.

“It is central to maintaining competitiveness, reducing operating costs, enhancing resilience to climate-related events, and meeting international expectations regarding environmental performance.

“Initiatives like the Nadi International Airport Solar Farm, therefore, deliver multiple benefits simultaneously,” Mr Gavoka said.

“They strengthen energy security, reduce emissions, support climate resilience, improve operation reliability, and contribute to long-term economic sustainability.”

The Civil Aviation Minister also highlighted contributions made by the national airway that aligned with the five-year framework that include exploring locally produced aviation fuel.

“Fiji Airways has progressively modernised its fleets through the introduction of Airbus A350 and Boeing 737 MAX, both of which deliver substantial fuel efficiency improvements compared with previous generation aircraft.

“The Government is also supporting work on sustainable aviation fuels. Fiji’s State Action Plan includes ongoing assessment of locally produced sustainable aviation fuel derived from sugarcane-based feedstocks.

“This demonstrates the breadth of Fiji’s approach to aviation decarbonisation and provides opportunities to create new economic activities while reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.”

He added capacity building of human capital within the sector was equally important and formed a significant part of the master plan.

The Civil Aviation Master Plan 2026 to 2031 was launched earlier this year.

item.title: Kiran blasts sign video
item.description: MINISTER for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran has condemned a video posted by students of a local tertiary institution that appears to mock sign language and the deaf community. Ms Kiran said sign language was an essential form of communication and an important part of the deaf community’s language, culture and identity.
item.content:encoded:
MINISTER for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran has condemned a video posted by students of a local tertiary institution that appears to mock sign language and the deaf community.

Ms Kiran said sign language was an essential form of communication and an important part of the deaf community’s language, culture and identity.

“Sign language is not a joke, a costume or a prop for entertainment,” she said.

“Making fun of it is disrespectful and reinforces the harmful attitudes and stereotypes that people with disabilities continue to face.”

Ms Kiran said every person, regardless of ability, had the right to dignity, equality and respect.

She said such incidents undermined efforts to remove barriers and build a more inclusive Fiji.

“True inclusion requires more than policies and programs.

“It requires each of us to examine our attitudes, challenge discrimination and ensure that people with disabilities feel respected, represented and valued in every part of society.”

She urged the students and institution to reflect on the harm caused and use the incident as an opportunity for education and accountability.

Ms Kiran also called on educational institutions to strengthen disability awareness and promote respect for diversity.

She said social media could either reinforce prejudice or help build a more inclusive society.

“Disability is not inability. Inclusion is everyone’s responsibility.”

item.title: Fiji exports first pilot shipment of homegrown agriculture produce
item.description: THE first pilot shipment of Fijian-grown agricultural produce has been exported to Naoero, marking a milestone in efforts to expand market opportunities for Fijian farmers across the Pacific. The shipment comprised 54 boxes of export-quality fruits, vegetables and root crops grown and harvested by farmers across Viti Levu. The consignment was exported under a MoU between the Pacific Islands Develo
item.content:encoded:
THE first pilot shipment of Fijian-grown agricultural produce has been exported to Naoero, marking a milestone in efforts to expand market opportunities for Fijian farmers across the Pacific.

The shipment comprised 54 boxes of export-quality fruits, vegetables and root crops grown and harvested by farmers across Viti Levu. The consignment was exported under a MoU between the Pacific Islands Development Forum (PIDF) and New Valley Processors (Fiji) Limited (NVPL), signed on July 23, 2026.

The produce included eggplants, long beans, telegraph cucumbers, English cabbage, cassava, watermelons, pineapples, tomatoes, taro leaves, taro, papayas, bananas, kumquats and lemons.

PIDF Secretary General Arpana Pratap said she was pleased with the quality of the produce and thanked NVPL for coordinating with farmers to meet the requirements of the first pilot shipment.

“The export of Fijian-grown agricultural produce to Pacific neighbours such as Naoero demonstrates that Fiji’s agriculture sector has the potential to expand beyond the local market,” Ms Pratap said. “This achievement would not have been possible without the support of our project partners, including NVPL, Nauru Airlines and the dedicated farmers,” she said.

The export of agricultural produce from Nadi to Northern Pacific markets is part of the Pacific Fresh AirLink (PFAL) initiative under the Food and Nutrition Security project coordinated by the PIDF.

The PFAL initiative was established to support the export of fresh agricultural produce from Fijian farmers to regional markets, creating new economic opportunities for local producers while improving access to fresh and nutritious food in Pacific communities.

NVPL chief executive officer Navitalai Tuivuniwai said the company had visited farmers across Viti Levu to ensure the produce met the required quality and quantity standards for export. “This first pilot shipment involved a lot of planning, discussions and meetings with farmers to ensure we could meet the deadline for the flight,” Mr Tuivuniwai said. “I am pleased that we were able to do so, and we will continue to work with the PIDF to export more produce to Northern Pacific markets. At the end of the day, our goal is to support and improve the economic livelihoods of our farmers.” Mr Tuivuniwai said NVPL also supplied seedlings to its network of farmers to help increase commercial production and processing of high-value crops and create new market opportunities for growers.

A Biosecurity Authority of Fiji official was also on site to conduct the required inspections before the consignment was loaded onto a Nauru Airlines flight that departed Nadi International Airport on August 18.

Export-quality Fijian produce packed into boxes for export to the Republic of Naoero as part of the first pilot consignment under the Pacific Islands Development Forum and New Valley Processors (Fiji) Limited partnership. Picture:SUPPLIED

item.title: State says evidence compelling
item.description: THE State has called for the conviction of Daniel Francis Prasad, arguing that overwhelming evidence proves he brutally murdered his wife Karishma Chaudhary with a cane knife outside their Nadi home. In closing submissions filed before Justice Aruna Aluthge at the High Court in Lautoka on Wednesday, State prosecutors Joeli Nasa and John Vaurasi submitted that Mr Prasad’s detailed admissions, physi
item.content:encoded:
THE State has called for the conviction of Daniel Francis Prasad, arguing that overwhelming evidence proves he brutally murdered his wife Karishma Chaudhary with a cane knife outside their Nadi home.

In closing submissions filed before Justice Aruna Aluthge at the High Court in Lautoka on Wednesday, State prosecutors Joeli Nasa and John Vaurasi submitted that Mr Prasad’s detailed admissions, physical evidence, and eyewitness testimony established his guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The court heard that on the morning of April 27, 2025, Mr Prasad confessed his actions to police officers arriving at the scene, stating he had chopped his wife and felt no regret.

Prosecutors highlighted that Mr Prasad confirmed his guilt across four separate stages of the investigation, including recorded caution interviews and a filmed crime scene reconstruction demonstrating how he used the blade.

Pathologist Dr Pranil Kumar testified that Ms Chaudhary died from severe sharp-force trauma to the head and neck.

The fatal blows involved substantial force, penetrating her skull and driving 10 millimetres into the brain.

A prosecution witness testified that after hearing screams and children crying, she looked out her window to see Mr Prasad holding a cane knife beside his wife’s bloodied body.

Taking the stand in his defence, Mr Prasad claimed he walked out of his kitchen to find two unknown men standing over his wife’s body.

He told the court that the men were having an affair with her and were the actual killers.

The State urged the court to completely reject Mr Prasad’s account as his defence failed to put this claim to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination, nor did he present an alibi.

The State submitted that the deliberate target of delicate body parts demonstrated a clear intention to kill, leaving no alternative verdict available to the court.

The court heard that the defence would be filing written closing submissions.

The matter has been adjourned to September 2 for judgment.

item.title: 3m cane target fuels jet future
item.description: FIJI will need to harvest 3 million tonnes of sugar cane to be able to supply feedstock needed to produce sustainable aviation fuel. Civil Aviation Minister Viliame Gavoka said this was one of the challenges they faced while implementing projects under the 2026-2031 Civil Aviation Master Plan.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI will need to harvest 3 million tonnes of sugar cane to be able to supply feedstock needed to produce sustainable aviation fuel.

Civil Aviation Minister Viliame Gavoka said this was one of the challenges they faced while implementing projects under the 2026-2031 Civil Aviation Master Plan.

“Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is challenging,” he said.

“We can make it in Fiji by using sugarcane as a feedstock, but then you will need to produce about three million tonnes of cane to produce the volume, the quantity of SAF that would make it economical and make us a producer of SAF in this part of the world.

“Those are some of the challenges that we have.”

In response, Lautoka Cane Producers Association president Bala Dass said producing a consistent 3 million tonnes of sugar cane each year was ambitious but possible with the right resources.

“Give the farmers what they need for that to happen,” said Mr Dass.

“And there has to be an improvement in all levels. FSC (Fiji Sugar Corporation) will need new high yielding and efficient mills, growers will need secured land tenure and the consistent work force to harvest that amount of cane.

“It is not impossible because at one point in time we used to produce more than 3 million to 4 million tonnes of cane.”

According to Government, between 2020 and 2024, annual sugar cane crushed had fallen from 1.73 million to 1.33 million tonnes.
